title: 3 Tricks Snakes Use to Swallow Meals Wider Than Their Heads
description:
How do snakes swallow prey wider than their own heads without choking? Their lower jaw halves are joined by a stretchy ligament and walk the meal in one side at a time, the windpipe opening pushes forward so they keep breathing, and their ribs only attach to the spine so the body stretches.

topic: How does a snake swallow something bigger than its head without choking?
script: Snakes never choke on meals wider than their own heads. Your jaw could never. So how? First, a myth. Snakes don't unhinge their jaws. The two halves of the lower jaw aren't fused at the chin. A stretchy ligament joins them, so they spread wide apart. Then each side moves on its own. Left grips, right slides forward, then left again. The snake basically walks its head over its meal. But with a mouth that full, how does it breathe? Its windpipe opening sits low in the mouth, and it can push forward and off to the side, like a built-in snorkel. And its ribs only attach to the spine, so the whole body stretches around the meal. King snakes can even swallow other snakes as long as themselves. So what's the biggest thing you think a snake could swallow?
key_facts: Snake jaws do not dislocate; the two lower jaw halves are not fused and are joined by elastic tissue (Live Science; NHM)
The two sides of the jaw move independently, ratcheting over the prey (king snake 'pterygoid walk', Live Science)
The glottis can move to allow breathing while swallowing large prey (WikiVet)
Snake ribs attach only to the spine (NHM)
King snakes ate corn snakes at least as long as themselves (Live Science)
